name: Coffee
title: From forest to coffeehouse
intro: Follow arabica from its East African roots through the Red Sea to the coffeehouses of London.
stops: Arabica coffee grew wild in Ethiopia. Its journey begins in the highlands, where the plant was already part of local life before it became a commodity traded across oceans.
A port gives coffee its name
Yemen became an early centre of coffee cultivation and trade. Merchants bought beans through Mocha, a Red Sea port whose name became associated with the drink.
Coffeehouses appeared in London in the mid-seventeenth century. A drink carried across trading networks gave customers a new place to meet, talk and exchange news.

sources.name: New York Botanical Garden · Coffeehouse cultures
Cambridge University Press · Coffee in the Red Sea area

name: Black pepper
title: The spice that crossed oceans
intro: Trace one branch of the pepper trade from India’s Malabar Coast around southern Africa to Lisbon.
stops: A market on the Malabar Coast
Kozhikode, historically called Calicut, was already a busy Indian Ocean port when Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498. Pepper grown in the region passed through established merchant networks.
Cape of Good Hope, South Africa
The Portuguese route linked the Atlantic and Indian Oceans by rounding southern Africa. Ships could carry pepper toward Europe without relying on the same chain of ports used in Mediterranean trade.
Portuguese merchants brought Malabar pepper to Lisbon. The route shifted part of the European trade toward Atlantic ports while other routes continued to operate.

sources.name: Kerala Tourism · Muziris and the spice routes
Trinity College Dublin · Did Vasco da Gama Matter for European Markets?

name: The potato
title: A highland crop crosses the Atlantic
intro: Follow a crop that Andean farmers diversified long before it reached Europe.
stops: A crop adapted to the highlands
Andean communities cultivated many kinds of potatoes. Different varieties and ways of preserving them helped make the crop a dependable food in the highlands.
Early records place potatoes in the Canary Islands in the sixteenth century. The islands offer a clue to how the crop travelled on shipping routes linking the Americas and Europe.
From a new arrival to a staple
Early records in mainland Spain include purchases for a hospital in Seville. Farmers and gardeners helped the crop spread over time, long before it became an everyday food across much of Europe.

sources.name: Cambridge University Press · Immigrant Potatoes
REDI research repository · Early history of the potato in Europe

name: Paper
title: How a craft travelled west
intro: Trace the spread of papermaking across workshops, trading cities and writing cultures.
stops: Papermakers in China learned to turn plant fibres into thin sheets. The craft could travel wherever people had suitable fibres, water and the knowledge to work them.
Samarkand became known for papermaking. A familiar story ties the craft’s spread to a single battle, but the route here shows centres of production without assigning the transfer to one event.
Papermaking reached Baghdad during the Abbasid era. Paper supported the work of scribes and book producers as the craft spread to other cities.
European papermakers developed their own workshop methods. Italian centres such as Fabriano became known for paper production and for using watermarks to identify sheets.

sources.name: UNESCO · Silk Roads arts and crafts
Vanderbilt Libraries · Papermaking in Europe and America

name: Transatlantic cable
title: When a message outran a ship
intro: Follow the 1866 telegraph cable from the Irish coast to Newfoundland, with a stop in the open Atlantic.
stops: A cable briefly worked in 1858 before failing. Engineers tried again, and in July 1866 the Great Eastern began paying out a new cable from Valentia.
A cable could break under its own weight as it sank. Crews had to control the rate at which it ran off the ship. An attempt in 1865 had already ended with a break at sea.
The cable reached Heart’s Content on July 27, 1866. Once connected to telegraph networks on both shores, news could cross the ocean in minutes instead of waiting for the next ship.

sources.name: World Heritage Ireland · Transatlantic Cable Ensemble
Smithsonian Libraries · The Underwater Web

name: The Silk Roads
title: From imperial capital to mountain corridors
intro: Follow one branch of the Silk Roads and see how people crossed deserts and mountain passes.
stops: Chang’an was a major capital at the eastern end of the corridor. Its markets drew merchants who connected the imperial city to regions far beyond it.
An oasis at the desert’s edge
Water and provisions made oasis towns crucial to travellers. The caves at nearby Mogao preserve evidence of the religious and artistic exchange that accompanied trade.
A meeting point in the Chu Valley
Suyab lay on routes through the western Tianshan region. Traders, rulers and religious communities all left traces along this corridor.

sources.name: UNESCO · Chang’an–Tianshan Corridor

name: Qhapaq Ñan
title: The roads that held an empire together
intro: Trace selected points of the Andean road network through mountains and high plateaus.
stops: Inca rule reached the northern Andes, where imperial roads linked centres in present-day Ecuador to a wider network that also incorporated older routes.
The network tied Cusco to administrative centres, settlements and storehouses. Runners could relay messages in stages across difficult terrain.
Roads crossed the open highlands near Lake Titicaca and continued into other regions. The network linked communities separated by altitude and distance.

sources.name: UNESCO · Qhapaq Ñan

name: China’s Grand Canal
title: How grain reached the capital
intro: Follow the waterways that connected southern production centres to northern cities.
stops: The canal connected the prosperous lower Yangtze region to markets farther north. Grain from the south could travel much of the way by water.
Near Huai’an, canal traffic encountered the Huai River system. Keeping the route navigable required water management as well as digging channels.
The waterway helped supply the northern capital. The canal connected the needs of the imperial court and city to agricultural regions hundreds of kilometres away.

sources.name: UNESCO · The Grand Canal

name: Canal du Midi
title: Finding water for a canal summit
intro: Cross southern France and discover how engineers kept a hilltop canal supplied.
stops: The canal starts at Toulouse, where it meets the Garonne river system. This connection made it part of a larger water route between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
At the summit, water could drain toward either coast. Feed channels brought water from the Montagne Noire to replace what lock operations consumed.
A lagoon opens to the Mediterranean
The canal reaches the Étang de Thau near Marseillan. The lagoon connects onward to the Mediterranean, where coastal shipping could take over.

sources.name: UNESCO · Canal du Midi

name: Rideau Canal
title: An inland route between two rivers
intro: Follow a canal built to connect Ottawa and Lake Ontario through rivers and lakes.
stops: Built in the early nineteenth century, the Rideau Canal gave British North America a route between the Ottawa River and Lake Ontario away from the border section of the St. Lawrence.
Instead of excavating the entire route, builders used lakes and rivers already on the landscape. Locks and dams joined navigable stretches and managed differences in height.
The route reached Kingston at Lake Ontario. A military supply route became a corridor for commerce and later for recreational boating.

sources.name: UNESCO · Rideau Canal

name: Panama Canal
title: Why ships climb above the sea
intro: Cross the isthmus on the original lock route and see why it relies on a freshwater lake.
stops: Water flows into successive lock chambers to raise vessels from the Atlantic side. Their destination is Gatún Lake, about 26 metres above sea level.
A lake becomes a shipping lane
Damming the Chagres River created a reservoir large enough to carry vessels across much of the isthmus. It also supplies water for the original locks.
After crossing the divide and descending at Pedro Miguel, ships reach Miraflores for the final descent on the original route. Each lock adjusts the water around the ship.

sources.name: Panama Canal Authority · Canal history

name: Suez Canal
title: A sea-level shortcut across Egypt
intro: Trace the cut linking the Mediterranean and Red Sea and see how it differs from a lock canal.
stops: The canal opened in 1869, giving ships a passage from the Mediterranean into Egypt’s isthmus of Suez. Before it opened, a sea voyage between Europe and the Indian Ocean went around Africa.
The canal crosses the Bitter Lakes. Their wider waters give ships more room than the narrow excavated portions of the passage.
At the southern end, vessels reach the Gulf of Suez and can continue into the Red Sea. Ships pass through at sea level without a flight of locks.

sources.name: Suez Canal Authority · Canal history

name: Semmering Railway
title: A railway learns to climb
intro: Travel from Gloggnitz to Mürzzuschlag on an early mountain railway.
stops: Work began in 1848 on a railway that would carry ordinary trains over the Semmering. The challenge was to climb steep terrain while keeping gradients manageable for locomotives.
Curves lengthened the climb, while viaducts and tunnels carried tracks across ravines and through ridges. The line’s shape records the engineers’ response to the landscape.
The line opened in 1854 and joined railways on either side of the mountains. Its bridges and tunnels demonstrated that rail could cross terrain once considered impractical for main lines.

sources.name: UNESCO · Semmering Railway

name: Rhaetian Railway
title: From Alpine valleys to Italy by rail
intro: Follow two railway lines across the Alps, from Thusis to Tirano.
stops: From Thusis the Albula line climbs through an Alpine valley. Loops and tunnels let trains gain height over a longer distance.
The Bernina line reaches its summit beside Lago Bianco. Steep gradients and tight curves allow a train to climb over the pass without a rack-and-pinion system.
The railway descends through the Poschiavo valley into Italy. At Brusio, a spiral viaduct lengthens the descent so the train can lose elevation within a small area.

sources.name: Rhaetian Railway · Albula and Bernina lines

name: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
title: A narrow-gauge climb into the Himalayas
intro: Follow the railway that connected the Bengal plains with Darjeeling’s high ridges.
stops: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway linked the plains to a hill town in the late nineteenth century. Narrow-gauge tracks helped it negotiate a route where a broad railway would have needed more space.
A summit on a winding route
Loops and reversing sections let the line gain height without a single sustained steep climb. Ghum sits near the highest point on the route.
A hill town becomes easier to reach
The railway brought passengers and supplies into Darjeeling. It tied the hill station and surrounding tea-growing district more closely to the plains below.

sources.name: UNESCO · Mountain Railways of India

name: Camino de Santiago
title: From the Pyrenees to Santiago
intro: Follow three points on the French Way, one of several routes used by pilgrims to Santiago.
stops: Travellers crossing the Pyrenees from France could find shelter at Roncesvalles. The mountain crossing made the availability of beds, food and care especially important.
A city on the pilgrimage road
Farther west, pilgrims crossed the city of Burgos. A long flow of travellers helped sustain institutions that offered hospitality along the route.
The cathedral in Santiago drew pilgrims from across Europe. The paths that converged on the city carried stories, customs and artistic ideas alongside travellers.

sources.name: Xunta de Galicia · The French Way

name: Kumano Kodō
title: A pilgrimage through Japan’s Kii Mountains
intro: Trace part of the Nakahechi route from the coast into the forested Kii Peninsula.
stops: Pilgrims travelling south along the coast reached Tanabe before turning inland. The route changes character here as it leaves the coast for valleys and steep ridges.
The shrine at Takijiri marks a traditional entrance to the mountain region. Smaller shrines along the path gave pilgrims places to stop and make offerings.
The path leads toward one of the three Kumano grand shrines. Climbing and walking through the forest were part of the pilgrimage experience.

sources.name: Tanabe City Kumano Tourism Bureau · Nakahechi

name: Oregon Trail
title: Across the Continental Divide by wagon
intro: Follow three points on the overland migration route to Oregon’s Willamette Valley.
stops: Many emigrants bought supplies and assembled wagon parties near the Missouri River. How much food, water and equipment a wagon could carry shaped the journey from the start.
A broad crossing of the Rockies
South Pass offered wagons a relatively gradual way over the Continental Divide. Travellers used Indigenous routes and knowledge as they crossed lands already home to Native nations.
Oregon City became an endpoint for many journeys. The movement brought new settlements and intensified the dispossession of Indigenous peoples.

sources.name: National Park Service · Oregon Trail

name: Lewis and Clark Expedition
title: Up the Missouri and out to the Pacific
intro: Follow three camps on the 1804–06 expedition and see how knowledge travelled with the party.
stops: The expedition spent the winter preparing near the junction of the Mississippi and Missouri rivers. In 1804 the party headed upstream on the Missouri.
The expedition wintered near Mandan and Hidatsa communities and drew on local knowledge. Sacagawea and Toussaint Charbonneau joined the party before it continued west.

After crossing the Rockies and travelling down the Columbia River system, the party spent the winter near the Pacific. Its journals recorded observations made along routes Native peoples already knew.

sources.name: National Park Service · Lewis and Clark Trail

name: Santa Fe Trail
title: A trading road across the plains
intro: Follow the mountain branch of a commercial trail that connected Missouri to New Mexico.
stops: William Becknell left the Franklin area in 1821 and opened a profitable trade with Santa Fe. Traders could exchange goods across the frontier with newly independent Mexico.
A trading post on the mountain route
This post on the Arkansas River linked merchants and Indigenous trading partners. Wagons could use the mountain branch to reach New Mexico via Raton Pass.
A market at the western end
Santa Fe connected overland commerce with older trade routes into Mexico. The goods unloaded here often continued onward with other merchants.

sources.name: National Park Service · Santa Fe Trail

name: Harriet Tubman’s journeys
title: Across a border in search of freedom
intro: Trace three places in Tubman’s life and the wider network that supported people escaping slavery.
stops: Tubman was born enslaved on Maryland’s Eastern Shore and escaped in 1849. She later returned to the region to guide others out of slavery.
Tubman reached Philadelphia, where abolitionists aided people who escaped slavery. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 raised the risk of recapture even in free states.
Tubman lived for a time in St. Catharines, where people who had escaped slavery established a community. Crossing into Canada placed them beyond enforcement of the U.S. fugitive slave law.

sources.name: U.S. National Archives · Harriet Tubman

name: Struve Geodetic Arc
title: Measuring Earth one triangle at a time
intro: Follow survey points from northern Norway to the Black Sea region.
stops: The Meridian Column marks the northern end of a nineteenth-century survey. Surveyors linked points by measuring angles between stations.

Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve worked at Tartu, which became a reference point for the survey. A chain of triangles allowed survey teams to calculate distances that were impractical to measure directly.
The arc ended near the Black Sea. The long measurement helped scientists estimate Earth’s size and shape with greater precision.

sources.name: UNESCO · Struve Geodetic Arc

name: Norse North Atlantic crossings
title: From Iceland to Newfoundland
intro: Follow selected points in the Norse expansion across the North Atlantic.
stops: Norse settlers established communities in Iceland. Islands provided places to settle and resupply as voyages extended farther into the North Atlantic.
Norse settlements grew in parts of Greenland where fjords offered landing places and nearby land supported grazing. Voyages could continue westward from these settlements.
Archaeologists found remains of Norse-style buildings and evidence of ironworking here. The site confirms that Norse seafarers reached North America around a thousand years ago.

sources.name: UNESCO · L’Anse aux Meadows

name: The Makasar trepang trade
title: A seasonal crossing to Arnhem Land
intro: Follow the sea-cucumber trade between Sulawesi and northern Australia.
stops: A port linked to Asian markets
Fishing crews set out from ports in what is now Indonesia to harvest trepang, or sea cucumber. Traders could sell the dried product onward into Asian markets.
Seasonal winds shaped when crews could sail south and when they could return. The voyages repeated across generations, creating regular contact across the sea.
Work and exchange on the coast
Crews processed trepang on the coast, where they traded and interacted with Aboriginal communities including Yolŋu people. Words, objects and accounts preserve traces of that contact.

sources.name: National Museum of Australia · Trade with the Makasar

name: Pony Express
title: How mail outran a single rider
intro: Follow the relay that carried mail across the American West before the telegraph took over.
stops: At St. Joseph, mail began the westbound relay. Riders carried compact mail bags because speed depended on keeping the load light.
Relay stations gave riders fresh horses at intervals. The network let mail travel through mountain and desert country faster than one horse could sustain.
A brief era of fast mail
Sacramento was the western end of the overland relay. Completion of the transcontinental telegraph in 1861 made the service unnecessary.

sources.name: National Park Service · Pony Express Trail

name: Greenwich time signals
title: How ships set their clocks from shore
intro: Follow a time signal from the Royal Observatory to ships and onward to the English Channel.
stops: The observatory began dropping a time ball in 1833. Its fall gave observers a visible signal they could use to set their clocks.
A later time ball at Deal received its signal by telegraph from Greenwich. Its drop relayed the observatory’s time to vessels offshore.
Ships at anchor off Deal could watch the ball drop and check their chronometers. Accurate time helped navigators determine longitude once at sea.

sources.name: Royal Museums Greenwich · Greenwich Time Ball
Royal Observatory Greenwich · Deal Time Ball

name: Incense across the Negev
title: How a caravan crossed the desert
intro: Follow three Nabataean settlements on the trade network that carried incense toward Mediterranean markets.
stops: A market on a desert branch
Mamshit stood on a branch of the Nabataean trade network. Caravans needed places to replenish supplies as much as they needed buyers for their cargo.
Avdat developed at a junction of desert routes. Fortifications, settlement remains and traces of farming show how a caravan stop could become a permanent community.
Haluza lay closer to the western end of the desert crossing. Towns like these allowed merchants to break a long journey into manageable stages.

sources.name: UNESCO · Incense Route in the Negev

name: Oman’s frankincense
title: From resin trees to seaborne trade
intro: Follow the supply network linking Dhofar’s frankincense trees to inland and coastal markets.
stops: Frankincense collectors cut into the bark of Boswellia trees and gathered the resin after it hardened. The dry hills of Dhofar supported the trees that made this trade possible.
The oasis at Shisr gave travellers a place to find water at the edge of the desert. Its position made it valuable to caravans carrying goods inland.
At Khor Rori, the settlement of Sumhuram gave traders access to the Indian Ocean. Frankincense could move in several directions through the inland and maritime network.

sources.name: UNESCO · Land of Frankincense

name: Camino Real de Tierra Adentro
title: A road built around silver
intro: Follow the inland road that carried silver, supplies and people through New Spain.
stops: From the capital, supplies and people travelled north. Silver returning from mining districts tied the road to trade through the capital and beyond.
Silver mining made Zacatecas a major destination. Mines and growing towns needed a steady flow of food, tools and workers across dry country.
An inland road becomes a corridor
The road continued north through Durango. Settlements, bridges and religious buildings along its branches record a route that also carried ideas and institutions.

sources.name: UNESCO · Camino Real de Tierra Adentro

name: The Zarafshan–Karakum corridor
title: Oases across Central Asia
intro: Travel west along a Silk Roads corridor shaped by rivers, oasis cities and desert crossings.
stops: A town in the Zarafshan valley
The valley gave travellers a way through mountain country. Ancient Panjakent preserves traces of Sogdian communities whose merchants helped connect distant markets.
Near Bukhara, Paykend served merchants on routes through the lower Zarafshan. Its position gave caravans a staging point before long stretches of desert.
A river crossing opens another route
At Amul, near modern Türkmenabat, travellers could cross the Amu Darya. From there routes led toward the Karakum and onward to other centres.

sources.name: UNESCO · Zarafshan–Karakum Corridor

name: Hadrian’s Wall frontier
title: How a frontier moved people and supplies
intro: Follow three points along Rome’s northern frontier in Britain.
stops: A fort at the river end
Segedunum stood near the Tyne at the wall’s eastern end. A fort here could oversee a frontier approach near a navigable river.
The fort at Housesteads occupied a ridge with wide views. Soldiers stationed there needed water, food and equipment brought into the frontier zone.
Birdoswald stood near the River Irthing. A fort helped control local movement, while civilian communities grew around the military presence.

sources.name: UNESCO · Frontiers of the Roman Empire

name: The Loire river corridor
title: How a river linked markets and estates
intro: Trace the middle Loire through cities and the country estates that grew along its banks.
stops: The Loire’s northward bend made Orléans a meeting point for river traffic and overland routes. Cargo could change hands here for the journey toward Paris.
Tours sits between the Loire and Cher. Access to water routes and fertile countryside helped support trade, towns and major estates in the valley.
Downstream, the river connected vineyard country and settlements with routes toward the Atlantic. The cultural landscape grew from the interaction between farming and transport.

sources.name: UNESCO · The Loire Valley

name: Port wine down the Douro
title: From vineyard terraces to the Atlantic
intro: Trace how wine moved from the steep upper Douro to warehouses near the river mouth.
stops: Terraces make steep hillsides workable and help hold soil in place. The wine began in a growing landscape shaped by generations of labour.
The Douro channel gave wine producers a route through difficult terrain. Régua grew as a centre for moving wine out of the interior.
Wine could be aged and prepared for export in cellars across the river from Porto. The journey linked a warm inland growing area with coastal trade.

sources.name: UNESCO · Alto Douro Wine Region

name: Tokaj wine
title: From autumn mist to hillside cellars
intro: Explore the connection between growing conditions, a network of cellars and Tokaj’s wine trade.
stops: Vineyards around Mád occupy slopes formed on volcanic terrain. The terrain creates differences in exposure, drainage and growing conditions over short distances.
Autumn moisture can favour noble rot under the right conditions. The fungus concentrates sugars in affected grapes, which can be gathered separately for sweet wine.
Tokaj stands where the Bodrog meets the Tisza. Cellars helped producers store wine, while the town’s river position connected the growing district to wider markets.

sources.name: UNESCO · Tokaj Wine Region

name: Champagne’s route to market
title: From chalk slopes to underground cellars
intro: Trace the landscape, storage and trade behind a sparkling wine.
stops: Around Hautvillers, hillside vineyards form part of the growing landscape. Slope and exposure influence how the grapes ripen.
Producers used underground cellars to store and mature wine. The cool, relatively stable conditions helped make lengthy ageing practical.
Reims became another production and trading centre. The houses and their cellars show how the industry combined rural growing, urban production and international distribution.

sources.name: UNESCO · Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars

name: Burgundy’s vineyard plots
title: How wine took the name of a place
intro: Follow the relationship between vineyard plots, trading houses and the institutions that shaped Burgundy’s wine country.
stops: A name for a small plot
The named vineyard plots known as climats capture differences in terrain and a long history of cultivation. A wine could be identified with a remarkably small area.
Beaune developed as a place where wine was made, stored and marketed. The town connected individual growers to buyers farther away.
Dijon’s political and administrative role helped shape the region’s landholding and wine economy. The vineyard names reflect centuries of social history as well as soil.

sources.name: UNESCO · Climats of Burgundy

name: The blue agave journey
title: From planted slopes to distillery
intro: Follow three towns in Jalisco’s agave landscape and see where growing ends and processing begins.
stops: Agave plants take years to mature. Their rows create a landscape where production follows the long growing cycle of a single crop.
Harvesters cut away the leaves to expose the heart. The hearts can then be cooked and processed to release fermentable sugars.
Distilling gives the town a wider reach
Distilleries turn the fermented liquid into a spirit. The growth of production tied the town’s workshops and labour to a market far beyond Jalisco.

sources.name: UNESCO · Agave Landscape of Tequila

name: Coffee in Colombia’s mountains
title: From hillside farms to a regional market
intro: Explore selected places in Colombia’s coffee landscape, where steep ground shaped farming and settlement.
stops: Coffee growers work a landscape of small farms and steep slopes. The terrain makes the way a crop is planted, harvested and moved especially important.
Towns like Filandia offered services and gathering places for nearby farming communities. Their streets and buildings reflect settlement linked to the coffee economy.
A larger hub for the region
Regional cities linked farming districts to wider commercial networks. Coffee travelled through layers of local and regional exchange on its way to distant buyers.

sources.name: UNESCO · Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia

name: Europe’s spa circuit
title: How people travelled for mineral water
intro: Follow three examples of the spa culture that spread through European travel, medicine and leisure.
stops: A city built around hot springs
Naturally heated water drew people to Bath for centuries. The later spa city added rooms, walks and public spaces for visitors who came to take the waters.
A resort grows around the cure
Thermal baths attracted visitors to Baden-Baden. Parks and entertainment made a stay part of social life as well as a course of treatment.
Colonnades sheltered people walking between springs. The buildings show how drinking mineral water became a shared ritual that reshaped resort towns.

sources.name: UNESCO · Great Spa Towns of Europe

name: Hanseatic Baltic trade
title: How merchants linked Baltic ports
intro: Follow three ports that show how merchants, ships and warehouses tied the Baltic together.
stops: Wismar grew as a Baltic trading town. Its harbour and town plan connected ships, warehouses and markets.
A crossing point on the coast
Stralsund’s position near the routes to Rügen helped it participate in Baltic exchange. Merchants used networks that linked many independent ports.
An island stop in the Baltic
Gotland’s position gave Visby access to routes across the sea. Its medieval warehouses and walls reflect the wealth and risks of long-distance trade.

sources.name: UNESCO · Historic Centres of Stralsund and Wismar
UNESCO · Hanseatic Town of Visby

name: Kilwa’s Indian Ocean trade
title: From inland gold to island ports
intro: Follow the trade network that made Kilwa a point of exchange between Africa and the wider Indian Ocean.
stops: Gold from the southern African interior reached coastal markets including Sofala. Merchants could then ship it north or exchange it for goods brought by sea.
An island harbour in the trade
Kilwa’s merchants gained wealth through trade including gold and ivory. Imported ceramics and other goods show how far the network reached.
Songo Mnara preserves stone houses and mosques. Together the two island settlements show how coastal trade helped sustain distinctive urban communities.

sources.name: UNESCO · Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara

name: Venice’s defensive network
title: Fortifying the roads and sea lanes
intro: Follow the places Venice fortified to hold routes across northern Italy and the Adriatic.
stops: Venice built substantial walls around Bergamo’s upper town. A fortified hilltop helped secure its position on the western side of the mainland territories.
Where a lake becomes a river
Peschiera stands at Lake Garda’s outlet into the Mincio. Its fortifications guarded a crossing and access to routes that used the lake and river.
Kotor’s position deep in the bay gave it shelter and a defensible approach. Its walls climbed the steep slopes above the harbour.

sources.name: UNESCO · Venetian Works of Defence

name: Portuguese Indian Ocean routes
title: Why three ports mattered to one empire
intro: Trace selected Portuguese strongholds between the east African coast, India and the Strait of Malacca.
stops: The island became a stopping point for Portuguese shipping on the east African coast. Ships could use it for shelter and supplies before continuing across the ocean.
An administrative base on a river
Goa became a centre of Portuguese administration in Asia. Its position on the Mandovi provided access to the coast and Indian Ocean trade.
Melaka occupied a strategic position on the strait connecting the Indian Ocean with waters farther east. Portuguese rule followed conquest of a city that was already a major trading centre.

sources.name: UNESCO · Churches and Convents of Goa
UNESCO · Island of Mozambique
UNESCO · Melaka and George Town

name: The voyage of the Batavia
title: A trading voyage cut short
intro: Follow the Dutch East India Company ship from departure to shipwreck and the survivors’ journey onward.
stops: The Batavia sailed from the Netherlands in 1628 carrying people, supplies and valuables. It was headed for the company’s trading base on Java.
The ship struck a reef off Western Australia in 1629. Survivors reached nearby islands, where access to water and supplies became urgent.
The destination reached in a small boat
The commander and a group of others sailed on in a ship’s boat to seek help at Batavia, now Jakarta. A rescue vessel later returned to the islands.

sources.name: Western Australian Museum · Batavia’s history

name: Cherokee Trail of Tears
title: A homeland taken by force
intro: Trace places connected with the forced removal of Cherokee people from their homelands in the 1830s.
stops: A capital and a disputed treaty
New Echota was a Cherokee capital. A treaty signed there by a minority faction became the U.S. government’s basis for removal despite opposition from most Cherokee people.
The landing was one departure point. Cherokee groups travelled by water or overland under conditions that caused illness and many deaths.
Tahlequah became a political centre of the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory. Cherokee people rebuilt institutions and communities after the forced migration.

sources.name: Cherokee Nation · Our Journey
National Park Service · Ross’s Landing

name: The 1877 Nez Perce flight
title: A forced journey toward Canada
intro: Follow three places in the flight of Nimiipuu bands who resisted removal to a reservation.
stops: The Wallowa Valley was home to Chief Joseph’s band. U.S. demands for removal helped set in motion a long flight eastward involving several bands.
U.S. troops attacked the camp at Big Hole. Many Nimiipuu people, including women and children, were killed, and survivors continued on.
A final siege near the border
The pursuit reached the Bear Paw Mountains, close to Canada. Some people escaped north, while others surrendered after a siege.

sources.name: Bureau of Land Management · Nez Perce Trail
National Park Service · Big Hole National Battlefield

name: The Anza expedition
title: A colonial route to San Francisco Bay
intro: Trace part of the 1775–76 overland expedition that brought settlers to northern California.
stops: The expedition travelled through Tubac, where Anza had served as commander. Families, soldiers and livestock made this a settlement expedition as well as a scouting journey.
Reaching California required a crossing of the Colorado River. The expedition passed through Quechan homelands and relied on Indigenous cooperation.
Anza explored the bay area for settlement sites. The expedition helped extend Spanish colonial power into lands already inhabited by Indigenous communities.

sources.name: National Park Service · Juan Bautista de Anza Trail

name: Iditarod freight trails
title: How winter linked Alaska’s towns
intro: Trace selected points on a historic trail system that moved mail, supplies and people across Alaska.
stops: Ships could unload people and freight at Seward. From the coast, routes led inland toward settlements and mining districts.
Knik served as a jumping-off point for trips inland. In winter, dog teams could move along packed snow and frozen waterways.
Trail branches helped move mail and freight to western Alaska. The network joined newer settlements with paths and travel practices already used by Alaska Native peoples.

sources.name: Bureau of Land Management · Iditarod National Historic Trail

name: Spain’s sheep trails
title: How herds moved with the seasons
intro: Follow the logic of seasonal grazing through the Spanish network of livestock routes.
stops: Herders could move sheep into cooler uplands when lowland pastures dried. Seasonal movement made use of grass available at different times of the year.
Broad rights of way called cañadas helped keep routes open for large flocks. Herders needed resting places and water as well as uninterrupted passage.
Lower and milder areas could support winter grazing. Moving between seasonal pastures connected rural economies across central and western Spain.

sources.name: UNESCO Tentative List · Mesta livestock trails

name: Italy’s shepherd tracks
title: From Apennine grass to winter plains
intro: Trace the route logic of transhumance between the central Apennines and Puglia.
stops: Flocks grazed in upland areas during the warmer months. As cold weather approached, shepherds could lead them toward lower ground.
A broad track through the hills
The drove roads, called tratturi, gave herders room to move many animals. Communities along the way provided places to rest, exchange goods and resupply.
The lower plains around Foggia offered grazing through milder months. Seasonal movement linked the plains to mountain communities and their wool economy.

sources.name: UNESCO Tentative List · Royal Shepherd’s Track

name: Coal through the Ruhr
title: From underground seam to river port
intro: Follow the links between mining, coke production and heavy transport in Germany’s Ruhr region.
stops: At Zollverein, shafts and machinery moved coal out of deep workings. Sorting and washing prepared it for further processing or shipment.
Heating coal with limited oxygen produced coke. Steelmaking depended on fuel that could withstand the heat and weight inside blast furnaces.
Duisburg’s port connects the Ruhr industrial area with the Rhine. Barges and railways made it possible to move the heavy raw materials and products of this regional economy in bulk.
